Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed, Spatial Triggers: Physical locations, Nighttime/Dark: Night-time or waking up in the dark
  Maladaptive Strategies: Smoking: I smoke, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Avoid Talking: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
The storm had come in with a violence Tavita could still taste: saltwater and burnt rubber coating his tongue, the sharp, acrid scent of wet insulation clinging to his clothes even after the rain stopped. He had been standing in the flooded driveway with his wife, Mara, when the sea wall collapsed. He remembered the exact moment the water crossed the threshold, the delay in the emergency broadcasts that stretched into agonizing silence, and the terrifying calm that followed. Now, years later, the memory rarely unfolded as a coherent narrative; it struck him as a fragmented scene so extreme it felt impossible that it had actually belonged to him. He would stand in the quiet of his kitchen and suddenly catch the ghost of that burnt insulation, his breath tightening. He could not stop what happened that day, and he had come to believe the world was a place where disaster waited behind every door. In the months that followed, Tavita moved his life inland, taking over a small accounting firm to rebuild a sense of order. As an auditor, his days became a strict routine of cross-referencing figures, a world where numbers behaved predictably. The habits of survival crept in. He began smoking a pack a day, the nicotine offering a brief pause before the vigilance resumed. He avoided relaxation because sitting still felt dangerous. He stopped speaking to anyone about the event or the aftermath, folding the grief into his chest instead of sharing it. His body tuned itself to a different frequency. When a room fell quiet, he assumed something dangerous was about to happen. When a client’s audit took longer than expected, he was certain a catastrophe was brewing behind the delay. He avoided specific physical locations, sticking only to familiar streets and buildings he had mapped out since the storm. He refused to enter unfamiliar spaces, telling himself he simply could not assess the danger in unknown layouts. Remaining within known routes offered a fragile calm, though the days still blurred into a hollow numbness that made him feel dead inside. His work required site visits, but a recent assignment to a sprawling, unfamiliar business park tested this boundary. He found himself standing in the lobby of Building C, unable to move past the security desk because the layout offered no clear sightlines to exits. He walked back to his car, circled the block, and called in sick. His refusal to visit unfamiliar client sites had become a professional boundary; partners noted his reliability on familiar properties but quietly passed him over for the regional director role, leaving him in routine compliance work. At home, the silence of the widowed house worked against him. Waking in the dark always sent his pulse racing, his mind replaying the collapse of the sea wall. He had come to believe that feeling happy or relaxed was a warning sign, a precursor to loss that made him immediately check the windows and straighten his shoulders. Tavita finally walked into the clinic because the numbness had grown too heavy to carry alone, and the constant scanning for danger left him exhausted. He was most afraid that the fear would never stop dictating his days, but he hoped to sit in a room without bracing for impact, and to one day let himself feel at ease without waiting for the other shoe to drop.
